chunks: "RAM is random-access memory, the read/write working memory of a system.
'Random access' means any location can be read or written in roughly the same time, regardless of address, and it's usually volatile, so it forgets everything when power is removed.
SRAM, static RAM, stores each bit in a six-transistor cell: two cross-coupled inverters that hold the value as long as power is applied, plus two access transistors that connect it to the bit lines.
It's fast, needs no refresh, and is used for CPU caches, register files, and the on-chip memory of microcontrollers, but a cell is large.
DRAM, dynamic RAM, stores a bit as charge on a tiny capacitor, with a single access transistor.
That's about a sixth of the transistors, so it's far denser and cheaper per bit, which is why main memory is DRAM.
But the charge leaks away in tens of milliseconds, so every row has to be periodically refreshed, and reading is destructive, so the sense amplifier has to write the value back.
It's also slower. So the trade is speed versus density: SRAM for the small, fast levels, DRAM for the large main memory."
